content.text: {"persuasion": "PERSUADED", "support_scope": "FULL", "rationale": "The book's core claim — that 'work' names a deed as such, morally underdetermined until context supplies whose command governs it and whether a wage is claimed — is directly carried by its printed texts and reconciles the Romans 4 / James 2 tension better than the strongest specific alternative. Exodus 18:20 distinguishes the commanded 'work that they must do' from the way walked; Micah 6:16 shows the identical noun applied to deeds governed by a rival lawgiver ('the works of the house of Ahab' kept under 'the statutes of Omri'), proving works are not intrinsically obedience; Luke 17:7-10 explicitly severs even complete obedience from wage-claim ('we have done that which was our duty'); Romans 4:4 itself uses wage-and-debt vocabulary ('the reward not reckoned of grace, but of debt'), so the book's reading of the contrast as faith versus wage-labor rather than faith versus obedience is textually native, not imported. James 2:21-22 ('by works was faith made perfect') then fits without strain. The common interpretation identifies the same referent (deeds) and is not a rival core; its polemical variant ('works' = self-righteous effort or obedience-as-basis) is the only reading that materially contradicts the book, and it cannot explain Micah 6:16's neutral usage, Luke 17:10's decoupling of obedience from wages, Psalm 111:7's parallel of God's own works with His commandments, or James's positive justification-by-works language without special pleading. No supplied text is better explained by a counter-reading than by the book's core.", "book_core_identification": "'Works' denotes deeds — acts as such — and is not a synonym for obedience or for self-righteous effort; the same deed becomes obedience when it executes God's command and disobedience when another lawgiver governs it, and even complete obedience earns no wage, so Romans 4 opposes faith to wage-claimed labor while James 2 presents the work as faith made visible.", "book_secondary_elaborations": ["The reading of Romans 4:4-5 as targeting specifically labor offered for wages/debt rather than obedience as a basis of justification", "The claim that Paul keeps two vocabularies distinct (God's law vs. traditions/commandments of men) and that 'works of the law' must be read contextually per passage (e.g., Galatians 2:16 inside the circumcision-party dispute)", "The linkage of works to commandment-keeping via Psalm 111:7 and Revelation 2:26 ('keepeth my works')", "The broader chapter's framework in which love, knowing, faith, and belief converge on commandment-keeping as one covenant response"], "strongest_counter_interpretation": "The classical Lutheran/Reformed polemical reading: in Paul's soteriological argument, 'works' functions as shorthand for human moral performance offered as a basis for standing before God — effectively obedience-as-merit — so that Romans 4:4-5 opposes faith to obedience itself as a justifying ground, not merely to deeds accompanied by a wage-claim; good works are then defined as the necessary fruit and evidence of faith, and 'works' apart from faith are intrinsically self-righteousness (Romans 4:4-5; 9:32; 11:6; Philippians 3:9; Isaiah 64:6).", "counter_core_identification": "'Works' are morally qualified deeds that evidence the inner state — good works being the fruit of grace and faith, evil works the fruit of the flesh — and in Paul's justification contexts 'works' stands for human obedience or effort offered as a ground of righteousness, which faith excludes.", "counter_relation_to_book_core": "SAME_CORE_BROADER", "material_core_denial": "The materially contradicting claim would be: works are intrinsically obedience (good works) or sin (evil works) — the noun itself carries the moral qualification — so Paul's exclusion of works from justification excludes obedience as such, and there is no neutral deed-category whose status is assigned by the governing lawgiver and the presence or absence of a wage-claim.", "counter_case": ["Romans 4:4-5 is traditionally read as opposing faith to any human doing as a justifying basis, with the wage image merely illustrating the principle of merit inherent in all works", "Romans 9:32 and 11:6 set works against grace categorically, suggesting 'works' as a soteriological class, not a neutral deed word", "The evidential fruit-of-faith framing (Matthew 7:16-20; Ephesians 2:8-10) is massively attested across traditions and treats good works as inherently expressive of regeneration, not as neutral deeds awaiting a lawgiver", "James 2 is handled in this tradition by distinguishing justification before God (faith) from vindication before men (works), preserving works as evidence only"], "book_explanatory_advantages": ["Micah 6:16 is decisive for the neutral-deed thesis: 'the works of the house of Ahab' are deeds condemned precisely because Omri's statutes, another lawgiver, govern them — the noun itself carries no fixed moral or soteriological charge", "Luke 17:7-10, printed with the entry, explicitly separates obedience from wage-entitlement: complete obedience still earns nothing, which blocks the equation of 'him that worketh' (Rom 4:4) with 'him that obeyeth' and shows Paul's target is the wage-claim, not obedience", "Exodus 18:20 defines the word at the law's first teaching as 'the work that they must do' — a deed specified by command, distinct from but ordered under obedience", "Psalm 111:7 and Revelation 2:26 show works paralleled with commandments and 'kept' like commandments, explaining why James can say faith is perfected by works without contradicting Romans", "The book resolves the Romans 4 / James 2 tension without positing two senses of 'justified' or treating James as a corrective to Paul: one word (deed), two contexts (wage-claim vs. faith-enactment)"], "counter_explanatory_advantages": ["Romans 9:32 and 11:6 ('if by grace, then no more of works') read most naturally as a categorical grace/works antithesis, which the polemical shorthand reading captures economically", "The fruit/evidence framing has overwhelming attestation (Matthew 5:16; 7:16-20; Ephesians 2:10) and directly explains why judgment proceeds 'according to works' (Revelation 20:12-13)", "It preserves the historic Protestant guardrail against merit theology with minimal interpretive machinery in the justification passages"], "evidence_book_core_cannot_explain": [], "comparative_winner": "BOOK", "decisive_sources": ["Micah 6:16 — the same noun 'works' applied to deeds governed by a rival lawgiver, proving works are not intrinsically obedience", "Luke 17:7-10 — complete obedience earns no wage, severing obedience from the wage-work Romans 4 excludes", "Romans 4:4-5 — Paul's own vocabulary is wages and debt, matching the book's identification of the target", "Exodus 18:20 — the word defined at the law's institution as the commanded deed, distinct from the way walked", "James 2:21-22 — works as faith made visible and perfected, coherent under the book's reading without a two-justifications device", "Psalm 111:7 — God's works paralleled with His commandments, showing works as commandment-shaped deeds"], "unresolved_objections": ["The book's contextual, passage-by-passage reading of 'works of the law' (especially Galatians 2:16 as bounded by the circumcision-party dispute) remains contested against both the traditional Reformed reading and the New Perspective, and the entry's texts do not adjudicate that debate", "Romans 9:32 and 11:6 are not among the printed texts, and the categorical grace/works antithesis there is handled by the book only via the wage-claim distinction, which a Reformed reader may find under-argued", "The chapter's broader synthesis binding works to commandment-keeping as the sole enactment of faith is a theological elaboration exceeding what the entry's six texts strictly establish"], "confidence": "high"}
